Relationship Between Environmental Factors and Plant Distribution and Diversity in the North African Sahara Region: The Case of Tunisian Senghar‐Jabess National Park
abstract: ABSTRACT The environmental factors influencing plant community composition in North African deserts are still not well described. This study evaluates the impact of environmental variables on vegetation structure in Senghar‐Jabess National Park (2804 km 2 ), a protected area situated in the hyper‐arid Sahara of southern Tunisia. Data collection was carried out from March 2023 to February 2024 in Senghar‐Jabess National Park using quantitative quadrat sampling. The study recorded 17 plant species belonging to 12 families. Ward's hierarchical clustering identified three distinct groups: erg and sandy soils (Group 1), sandy regs (Group 2), and skeletal soils (Group 3). Across 20 abiotic variables, elevation, annual mean temperature, and distance to water sources accounted for 39%, 33%, and 24% of the variation among groups, respectively. Canonical correspondence analysis indicated that pH, electrical conductivity, distance to water sources, and UTM Northing significantly affected species composition ( p < 0.01). Fine sand and silt contents were diagnostic as important secondary gradients. The results demonstrate that geomorphological and edaphic factors influence species assembly in this extreme desert environment. The ordination also supports the hypothesis that erosion‐induced texture changes act as powerful abiotic filters shaping community composition. The CCA results demonstrate that erosion‐induced shifts in soil texture are fundamental drivers of vegetation differentiation and land degradation dynamics in desert ecosystems. These findings offer an ecological foundation for biodiversity conservation and sustainable land degradation management in the Saharan ecosystem.

title: Unraveling the Driving Mechanisms Behind Spatial–Temporal Evolution of Low‐Efficiency Cropland in Wildland‐Urban Interface: Evidence From Wuhan, China
abstract: ABSTRACT Cropland fragmentation and abandonment are critical global issues which have hindered the improvement of cropland utilization efficiency, undermining agricultural sustainability. In the context of rapid urbanization, cropland efficiency, especially within the wildland‐urban interface (WUI), is facing increasing challenges. Taking the WUI of Wuhan city as the research area, this study comprehensively incorporates cropland fragmentation and cropland abandonment to quantitatively evaluate the degree of low‐efficiency cropland. On this basis, the XGBoost‐SHAP model is adopted to systematically explore the driving mechanisms from natural and socio‐economic dimensions. The results show that: (1) During 2004–2024, the WUI expanded significantly, with a stabilizing growth rate since 2014. (2) Cropland fragmentation is the primary manifestation of low efficiency of cropland in the WUI, and cropland abandonment initially increased but later decreased. Both of them exhibit spatial heterogeneity in northern and southern Wuhan. (3) The distribution centroid of low‐efficiency cropland has been shifting to the northeast direction since 2014. (4) Low‐efficiency cropland in WUI stems from complex interactions, with spatial conflict between construction land and cropland playing a dominant role, while the influence of natural factors gradually diminishes over time. This study has important implications for identifying urban fringe areas and optimizing land‐use efficiency.

title: Agroforestry, Climate Resilience, and Land Degradation in OECD Economies: Roles of Innovation and Finance
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite the growing prominence of agroforestry practices in environmental research, its specific impact on climate‐induced land vulnerability, land degradation, and territorial carbon dioxide emissions is insufficiently explored in OECD economies. This study investigates how nonlinear effects of agroforestry practices, financial markets, innovation, environmental taxes, along with final consumption expenditure, determine territory‐based carbon emissions in OECD countries over the period 1994–2021. This study applied the second‐generation Driscoll–Kraay technique to analyze the data, while quantile regression serves as a nonparametric approach as a robustness check. The results show that agroforestry has inverted‐U shaped curve underlying that agroforestry in the initial stages may cause land degradation while at the later stages, it supports the climate resilience practices and land restoration in OECD economies. Moreover, financial development exerts heterogeneous effects in both models, suggesting differing channels of support for financial development. Green innovation and environmental taxes significantly reduce territorial carbon emissions, while final consumption expenditure, as theoretically expected, increases it. The results show robustness through nonparametric quantile regression with the role of income. Policy implications emphasize the adaptive framework of financial mechanisms, innovation, and environmental taxation to support agroforestry practices in a customized yet constantly focused manner on the reduction of emissions while supporting the development of climate resilience strategies in OECD economies.

title: On the intersection of Black geographies and policy mobilities: Tracing circuits of anti-racism in Newcastle upon Tyne
abstract: This paper reflects theoretically on the intersection of Black geographies and policy mobilities by tracing the historical and contemporary movements of Black activists, intellectuals and anti-racist struggles in Newcastle upon Tyne. While Black geographies foregrounds Black spatial imaginaries, resistance and epistemologies rooted in racial capitalism and coloniality, it has insufficiently interrogated how racialized policy formations and their circulations function transjurisdictionally. Likewise, policy mobilities, which charts the movement and mutation of urban policy models across contexts, offers an opportunity to expose the racialized structures underpinning these movements. This paper develops a conceptual approach that examines how race and power circulate through circuits of racialized spatial practices, Black actors and political thought and anti-racist struggles. The paper traces how Black individuals, ideas and infrastructures – routed through historical visits by Martin Luther King Jr., Frederick Douglass and Muhammad Ali as well as through contemporary cultural programs like Freedom City and protest movements like Black Lives Matter – are mobilized within and beyond the urban. In so doing, it advances a global, relational understanding of Black spatial politics that provokes a rethinking of urban theory’s Euro-American biases.
journal_name: Environment and Planning C: Politics and Space

title: Branding cities or citizens? Virtue-based branding as a technology of subjectification in Louisville
abstract: City branding is increasingly understood as shaping not only how cities are seen but who their residents become. This paper contributes to the growing scholarship that conceptualizes place branding as a technology of subjectification, arguing that when a city is branded with a human attribute, it is in effect its citizens who are branded. Drawing on a qualitative case study of Compassionate Louisville, the research traces how compassion was institutionalized as a governing discourse following the city’s formal adoption of the brand identity. The study reveals how the brand narrative operates simultaneously as a moral ideal, a performative expectation, and a political resource used to legitimize policy and manage social contradictions. By framing compassion as an apolitical, universal virtue, the brand establishes a disciplinary framework that encourages self-regulation and moral conformity while depoliticizing systemic social suffering. The paper contributes to debates within political geography and urban studies by demonstrating how virtue-based branding acts as an affective technology of power, reshaping urban subjectivities.
journal_name: Environment and Planning C: Politics and Space

title: Novel CRISPR therapy is poised to gain first FDA approval to alter genes inside the body
Revisiting new accounting history four decades on: reconciling traditional and critical historiographies
abstract: Purpose Revisiting debates in New Accounting History four decades on, this paper advances accounting historiography through the development of a Neo-Critical Accounting History (NCAH) framework that systematically integrates the strengths of traditional accounting history with the theoretically informed and critical orientation of new accounting history. In answering the “how” question, the framework offers an analytical pathway through which accounting historians may proceed with a rigorous and socially attuned mode of inquiry. Design/methodology/approach The study is grounded in critical accounting approach, in particular, Habermas's method of rational reconstruction (Held, 1980) providing the philosophical foundation for proposing an agenda advancing framework for NCAH. The framework integrates the methods of historical academic monograph with key features of both traditional and new accounting history. Findings The proposed NCAH framework is articulated across three interrelated dimensions. First, it integrates traditional and critical historiography by combining historical rigour with critical depth to recover marginalised voices and enhance contextual analysis. Second, it advances epistemic pluralisation through rigorous source critique, methodological triangulation, and engagement with diverse archival and counter-accounts, thereby addressing archival silences, partialities, and power relations. Third, it embraces theoretical openness and contemporary relevance, enabling historical inquiry into emerging accounting-related topics aligned with broader societal and ethical concerns, and strengthening accounting history's engagement with contemporary scholarly and public debates. Originality/value The manuscript demonstrates how traditional and new accounting history approaches may be systematically integrated, including through approaches inspired by abductive reasoning. Within this framing, narrative is positioned not as an end in itself, but rather as a point of departure for deeper theoretical interpretation and historical analysis. In doing so, NCAH reconciles historical and archival rigour with theoretical openness, thereby enhancing the analytical depth of the discipline and its capacity to contribute to interdisciplinary scholarship, societal reflection, and professional practice.

title: Between the hammer and the anvil: Collaborative states, MNES and development
abstract: Most governments continue to attract MNE investment as the optimal means of achieving economic development. However, MNEs have had a patchy record in addressing inequalities. Contemporaneously, the zeitgeist over the last decade has leaned toward greater state interventionism as part of inward-looking domestic policies, where the state is the main actor shaping economic development. We argue that successful developmental outcomes require neither the hollowing out of the state nor heavy-handed interventionism, but rather a collaborative state that strategically coordinates the MNE-state nexus. MNEs do not generate positive development outcomes through market mechanisms alone, just as states cannot always substitute for market actors through direct intervention. Instead, development emerges from a calibrated symbiotic relationship where the state creates location advantages, builds absorptive capacity, and coordinates linkages between MNEs and domestic actors, while managing diverse stakeholder interests and avoiding regulatory capture. We identify two critical prerequisites for effective collaboration: (1) a Weberian technocratic bureaucracy insulated from political volatility, and (2) a developmental consensus among domestic interest groups that prioritizes long-term national upgrading over short-term gains.

title: Gaze Behavior in Pedophilia and Hebephilia: How Task Instruction and Sexual Interest Shape Viewing of Prepubescent and Pubescent Stimuli
abstract: Abstract Visuospatial attentional processes are central in eye-tracking research of deviant sexual interest, yet it remains unclear to what extent task instructions modulate early (time to first fixation; number of first fixation) and late visuospatial attention (relative fixation time). We examined gaze behavior in individuals with pedophilic, hebephilic, and teleiophilic sexual interests while viewing prepubescent, early pubescent, and adult stimuli under free-viewing and forced-choice (attractiveness rating) conditions. We additionally assessed viewing time (VT) as an established indirect measure of sexual interest. Pedophilic and teleiophilic participants showed earlier orienting toward their preferred age category, whereas gaze patterns in the hebephilic group were inconsistent and differed from the VT results. Late visuospatial attentional indices such as relative fixation time indicated that pedophilic participants fixated roughly equally across all age categories, whereas hebephilic and teleiophilic participants fixated longer on adult stimuli. Within the present experimental design, the forced-choice condition was associated with more pronounced group-related effects and shorter times to first fixation, irrespective of group and stimulus type. These findings may provide preliminary indications of the potential sensitivity of this task context for early visuospatial attention, while alternative explanations and limitations of the experimental design are discussed. This study contributes to the limited eye-tracking literature on deviant sexual interest by explicitly considering both pedophilic and hebephilic sexual interest.

The Welfare Effects of Price Shocks and Household Relief Packages: Evidence from an Energy Crisis
abstract: Aggregate price shocks generate unequal welfare losses both across and within income groups.Policymakers face a trade-off: price subsidies direct more support to households facing larger losses, but create inefficiencies, while transfers are less distortionary but harder to target.We develop and implement a framework to quantify this trade-off using rich panel data on households' energy spending and incomes, alongside price and policy variation from the 2022-23 European Energy Crisis.Absent policy intervention, average household welfare losses would have equalled 6% of income, with some households facing much larger losses.The combination of an energy-price subsidy and universal transfers reduced both the mean and dispersion of losses, but incurred efficiency costs equal to 12% of total relief-package revenue costs.Optimal policy entails a strictly positive price subsidy, though its level is lower when transfers can be targeted using income and prior energy usage.

title: Noisy Global Value Chains
Climate Risk Disclosure and Risk Sharing in Financial Markets
abstract: Abstract In this paper, I model how climate risk disclosure impacts climate risk sharing among investors. I show that this disclosure can improve risk sharing by helping investors identify stocks that effectively hedge climate risk, and I analyze the disclosure’s impact on investors’ equilibrium portfolio choices. I then study firms’ voluntary disclosure incentives and analyze when disclosure mandates enhance risk sharing. Finally, I demonstrate that, by facilitating risk sharing, climate risk disclosure reduces the climate risk premium among stocks held by climate-focused investors. Hence, disclosure can lower the valuations of firms with low climate exposures and the overall market. (JEL: D82, D84, G12, G14)

The technological-financial-military linkage and the reproduction of inequality between countries
abstract: In recent years, military power has re-emerged as a central driver of international economic relations. Economic theories have largely dismissed militarism as irrational rent-seeking that distorts efficient markets or they have focused predominantly on its impact on domestic economic performance. Both these perspectives, however, overlook the mutually reinforcing dynamic between military power and the reproduction of global economic asymmetries. Instead, this paper introduces what we term the imperialist feedback loop, which operates as follows: the technological and financial dominance of core economies provides the foundation for military dominance, which is then instrumental to reproduce the asymmetric global division of labour underpinning technological and financial dominance itself. Empirically, we employ a hidden Markov model to dynamically cluster country panel data (1988-2023), identifying a stable hierarchical world structure, wherein the stability of the imperialist core is tied to the existence of an impoverished periphery and limited upward mobility from the semi-periphery. The empirical validation of militarism's core role in reproducing imperialist structures can inform the design of policies aimed at counteracting the technological-military dependency of less-developed countries, ultimately reducing global inequalities.

Government Guarantees and Dynamic Debt Runs
abstract: Abstract This study quantifies the impact of public guarantees on the stability of bank wholesale funding. We study the Chinese market for negotiable certificates of deposit (NCDs) around the first bank failure in two decades, the Baoshang event, which struck investors’ belief in government guarantees on wholesale bank debt. We document a sharp increase in NCD spreads, issuance failures, and runs, with weaker banks becoming more exposed to rollover risk after the event. Using a model of dynamic debt runs, we estimate that the perceived guarantee fell from 54% of creditor losses before the event to approximately zero after the event. The decline is largest for small banks, low-rated banks, and rural commercial banks. Our structural model also allows us to compare alternative policies aimed at stabilizing creditors’ willingness to roll over short-term debt.

title: The Price of Simplification: What We Miss When Hedonic Price Variation is Ignored
Industrialization, class conflict, and the closing window of democratic opportunity
abstract: Abstract This paper addresses two long-standing questions in the political economy of development: how the timing of industrialization affects the transition to democracy and how different social classes shape that transition. We develop a sequential game among landed elites, industrialists, and workers embedded in a growth model with endogenous industrialization. The model identifies a window of democratic opportunity during which the industrial class prefers democracy to industrial autocracy. Whether democracy occurs depends on two dimensions of workers’ de facto political power: their power against the landed class determines when industrialization occurs and when landed rule ends; their power against the industrial class determines when the democratic window closes. Later industrialization therefore makes democratization less likely but not impossible. A calibration to Great Britain and numerical exercises for early and late industrializers show that the revolt threat required to sustain democracy rises as industrialization is delayed. Faster technological growth advances political transitions but does not, by itself, determine whether democracy or industrial autocracy follows landed rule.

title: Constant Connectivity as Everyday Practice: Theorizing Through Problematization
abstract: Abstract Despite a significant amount of research on constant connectivity , defined as the opportunity to remain connected to work at any time, from any place, we assert that there remains a disconnect between how constant connectivity is studied and how it unfolds in everyday occurrences. Using the miner‐prospector continuum, we problematize the extant literature to evaluate this assertion and develop new theory. Our mining reveals that constant connectivity studies rely on notions of time and place that insufficiently demarcate work–nonwork boundaries; prescribe constant connectivity as either wholly incompatible with enacting nonwork roles or inherently interfering with specific nonwork activities; and operationalize constant connectivity with vague ‘technology use’ constructs. In prospecting, we conceptualize constant connectivity as a set of sociomaterial practices that capture how: technology affords opportunities to engage in, and disengage from, work activity; constant connectivity and nonwork role enactment are compatible via the pursuit of work and nonwork activities in parallel or sequentially; and work–nonwork boundaries are socially constructed in ways that transcend time and place. Taken together, we extend considerations of constant connectivity beyond knowledge workers to any occupation (skilled trades; physical labour) in which individuals use technology to conduct aspects of work at any time, from any place.

title: Explaining Coexisting Trust and Distrust Transitions: The Case of Senior Doctors in the UK NHS
abstract: Abstract The emergence of distrust in organizations damages working relationships and leads to poor organizational performance. We examine how senior doctors in the UK NHS transitioned from low trust/low distrust to low trust/high distrust in their managers and employer. Drawing on qualitative data from three time periods, we show, counter‐intuitively, how a positive crisis response by doctors' leaders during COVID‐19 intensified a long‐term downward trust–distrust trajectory. This response temporarily restored confidence and elevated expectations of a renewed psychological contract among doctors. When those expectations were later violated, scepticism and value incongruence grew, inciting negative expectations and a descent into distrust. We make three contributions to trust–distrust theory. First, we identify a previously unexplained pathway from coexisting low trust/low distrust to low trust/high distrust through a temporary state of high trust/low distrust. Second, we explain how ideological contract violations, perceived betrayals of core values and professional identities, drive the development of distrust. Third, we extend punctuated‐threshold explanations of distrust emergence by demonstrating that distrust can arise not only from accumulating negative experiences but also from the collapse of newly restored positive expectations. This has broader implications for the leadership of change, particularly the management of hope and expectations during crisis.

title: Insurers’ Investments and Insurance Prices
abstract: We develop a theory in which stable funding from insurance underwriting allows insurers to earn the liquidity premium on illiquid assets and pass part of it back to policyholders through lower prices. Consistent with the model’s predictions, we show empirically that (1) insurance prices are lower when the liquidity premium is higher, for both life insurers and property and casualty insurers. (2) In the cross-section, insurers with more stable funding earn higher expected returns and set lower prices. (3) It is specifically the part of expected returns driven by stable funding that passes through to prices. The findings highlight the value of insurance underwriting as a stable source of funding, with benefits that flow back to policyholders. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: The authors acknowledge support from the FRIC Center for Financial Frictions [Grant DNRF102]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.09038 .

title: Comparing Factor Models Under Regime Switching
abstract: We compare factor pricing models using the “test-asset irrelevance” result but under regime switching. We show that the unconditional squared Sharpe ratio measure is no longer appropriate for model comparison when returns are subject to regime shifts. However, conditional on a given regime, model comparison can be performed using the conditional squared Sharpe ratio metric. We find that the Fama-French six-factor model that employs a cash-based profitability factor, the Barillas-Shanken six-factor model, and the Stambaugh-Yuan four-factor model are jointly the best-performing models under the bull regime. However, no model performs significantly better than others under the bear regime. Importantly, these findings are robust to regime uncertainty. We also find that unconditional model rankings closely mirror those in bull markets, overstating the superiority of the models identified as best performing in expansions by ignoring the performance convergence across models that emerges in downturns. This underscores the importance of evaluating factor models conditional on market regimes. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.04942 .

title: What’s at Stake? Understanding the Role of Home Equity in Flood Insurance Demand
abstract: Changing flood insurance demand shifts climate risk across homeowners, lenders, and governments. We show that flood insurance take-up follows rising and falling home equity over the housing boom and bust across markets with different price dynamics. To isolate the causal effect of risk shifting on insurance demand, we study flood insurance policy renewals over the housing bust, exploiting granular differences in purchase timing that led policyholders to experience differential changes in skin-in-the-game exposure to flood risk for the same change in home equity. When homeowners have less equity exposure to flood losses, they are less likely to renew their policies. Lenders, in turn, have little incentive to require flood insurance when they can sell their mortgages to federally backed mortgage purchasers. This paper was accepted by Tomasz Piskorski, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01302 .

title: The Data-Driven Censored Newsvendor Problem
abstract: We study a censored variant of the data-driven newsvendor problem, where the decision maker must select an ordering quantity that minimizes expected overage and underage costs based only on offline censored sales data rather than historical demand realizations. Our goal is to understand how the degree of historical demand censoring affects the performance of any learning algorithm for this problem. To isolate this impact, we adopt a distributionally robust optimization framework, evaluating policies according to their worst-case regret over an ambiguity set of distributions. This set is defined by the largest historical order quantity (the observable boundary of the data set), and contains all distributions matching the true demand distribution up to this boundary while allowing them to be arbitrary afterward. We demonstrate a spectrum of achievability under demand censoring by deriving a natural necessary and sufficient condition under which vanishing regret is an achievable goal. In regimes in which it is not, we exactly characterize the information loss due to censoring: an insurmountable lower bound on the performance of any policy, even when the decision maker has access to infinitely many demand samples. We then leverage these sharp characterizations to propose a natural robust algorithm that adapts to the historical level of demand censoring. We derive finite-sample guarantees for this algorithm across all possible censoring regimes and show its near-optimality with matching lower bounds (up to polylogarithmic factors). We moreover demonstrate its robust performance via extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world data sets. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.09021 .

title: Rethinking Distribution Shifts: Empirical Analysis and Modeling for Tabular Data
abstract: Different distribution shifts require different interventions, and algorithms must be grounded in the specific shifts they address. However, methodological development for robust algorithms typically relies on structural assumptions that lack empirical validation. Advocating for an empirically grounded data-driven approach to algorithm development, we build an empirical testbed comprising natural shifts across 8 tabular data sets, 172 distribution pairs over 45 methods, and 90,000 method configurations encompassing empirical risk minimization and distributionally robust optimization (DRO) methods. We find that Y|X-shifts are most prevalent in our testbed, in stark contrast to the heavy focus on X (covariate)-shifts in the machine learning literature, and that the performance of robust algorithms is no better than that of vanilla methods. To understand why, we conduct an in-depth empirical analysis of DRO methods and find that underlooked implementation details—such as the choice of underlying model class (e.g., LightGBM) and hyperparameter selection—have a bigger impact on performance than the ambiguity set or its radius. We illustrate via case studies how a data-driven understanding of distribution shifts can provide a new approach to algorithm development. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08298 .

title: Banking on a Corporate Rebrand
abstract: Firms often rebrand to counter negative shocks, but can it work? Using a historical natural experiment, we analyze a large sample of companies from the same industry (banking) that shared very similar names, but overwhelmingly decided to change them in response to a common, negative news shock. U.S. entry into World War I in 1917 created a sudden anti-German backlash against anything that invoked an association with the now enemy. The shock itself was thus orthogonal to bank fundamentals and pre-existing trends, but pushed banks to reconsider their brands. After 1917, the few German-named banks that kept their tainted names saw significant declines in assets, deposits, and market share relative to other banks. However, German-named banks that rebranded mitigated much of the negative shock. Specifically, German-named banks that adopted a new non-ethnic brand name avoided between 75% and 85% of the anti-German effect, and those that adopted a new patriotic brand name were able to neutralize it completely. Overall, we find that “crisis rebranding” paid off in our historical setting regardless of the chosen brand, with patriotic rebranding proving the most effective at offsetting the exogenous shock. This paper was accepted by Jean-Pierre Dube, marketing. Funding: K. J. Mitchener thanks the Ciocca Center for Entrepreneurship and Innovation at Santa Clara University for funding this research (Grant 2024-CIOG11). Any views expressed in this paper exclusively represent those of the authors and do not reflect the official viewpoint of the Oesterreichische Nationalbank, the European Central Bank, or the Eurosystem. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03635 .

title: The Economics of Waste Valorization
abstract: As the spread of waste imposes substantial environmental and economic burdens, a newer operational strategy, waste valorization, is gaining attention. This approach transforms production-generated byproduct waste into valuable, distinct products, creating intricate production and demand interdependencies that traditional strategies like remanufacturing and coproduction cannot fully capture. In this study, we examine the impacts of these interdependencies within a two-stage stochastic production decision model to determine optimal production quantities under waste valorization. Our findings reveal that a higher waste valorization rate does not always benefit the manufacturer, especially if the waste incurs disposal costs. When product demands are uncorrelated, the manufacturer’s optimal profit can exhibit an inverse U-shaped relationship with the valorization rate, attaining its maximum at a moderate level that maintains a perfect balance in production. Conversely, when product demands are correlated, the manufacturer employs a “pool-to-center” strategy, using different pooling policies to smooth production quantities and minimize disparities with respect to the valorization rate. Surprisingly, as demand randomness or correlation intensifies, the optimal profit becomes M-shaped, with profit maximum shifting toward either low or high valorization rates, a phenomenon we term “go-to-extreme.” Although waste valorization can yield both economic and environmental benefits, we caution that a more efficient waste valorization process may lead to negative outcomes for both the manufacturer and the environment. This analysis not only sheds light on how waste valorization contributes to waste reduction and economic value, but also provides insights for production decision making. This paper was accepted by Caroline Flammer, sustainability. Funding: Financial support from the National Science Foundation of China [Grants 72301055, 72322017, 72471244, and 72101102] is gratefully acknowledged. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08500 .

title: Who Will be Assigned Unreasonable Tasks by Supervisors: A Conjoint Survey Experiment
abstract: ABSTRACT Supervisors sometimes assign employees tasks that employees may perceive as unreasonable because they fall outside their formal job duties. Prior research has mostly focused on the negative effects of unreasonable tasks on employee outcomes, without examining the fundamental question of who is more likely to be assigned such tasks by their supervisors. To answer this question, we examined three distinct logics underlying the assignment of unreasonable tasks based on employee attributes (i.e., age, gender, task performance, helping behavior, recent workload, and relationship closeness): stereotype‐driven logic, efficiency‐driven logic, and exchange‐driven logic. In a fully randomized conjoint survey experiment, we asked 464 supervisors to allocate an unreasonable task based on evaluations of 4640 hypothetical employee profiles, with profiles varying randomly on six employee attributes. Results show that supervisors are more likely to assign unreasonable tasks to younger employees who perform better on tasks, exhibit more helping behavior, currently have lighter workloads, and maintain closer relationships with their supervisor. The relatively stronger effects of employees' recent workload, task performance, and helping behavior suggest that the efficiency‐driven logic plays the most influential role in shaping supervisors' unreasonable task assignments. We discuss the theoretical, methodological, and practical implications of our findings.

title: Incumbents’ Alliances and (Non-)Adaptation During the Pre-Commercialization Stage of a New Technology
abstract: Research on incumbent adaptation through alliances typically assumes that incumbents can entice partners to share proprietary knowledge in a new technology by offering access to valuable complementary assets. This assumption fits the commercialization stage of a new technology, when both proprietary knowledge and complementary assets hold high value. However, during the pre-commercialization stage—when proprietary knowledge in the new technology is valuable but incumbents’ complementary assets cannot yet be fully deployed to commercialize the new technology—this logic may not hold. We develop a framework that explains how stage-dependent shifts in the value of both proprietary knowledge and complementary assets alter the bargaining power between incumbents and knowledge-possessing firms, thereby reshaping the adaptive potential of alliances. Using data on the semiconductor industry during the emergence of nanotechnology, we found that alliances between semiconductor incumbents and nanotechnology-capable partners are less likely to form and, even when formed, are less likely to focus on the explicit transfer of proprietary knowledge in emerging nanotechnology. Moreover, these alliances are more likely to be structured as joint ventures, especially when the risk of knowledge leakage is heightened. Joint venture arrangements, in turn, impede semiconductor incumbents’ post-alliance nanotechnology invention more than contractual arrangements. Taken together, we develop insights into how incumbents may struggle to use alliances for adaptive learning during the pre-commercialization phase of a new technology.

title: Wrongdoers or Saviors? CEO Activism, Media Partisanship, and the Media’s Construction of CEO Infamy and Celebrity
abstract: This study advances research on social evaluations by theorizing how partisan media construct CEO infamy through dramaturgical logics distinct from those underlying CEO celebrity. Moving beyond conceptualizations of infamy as merely negative celebrity, we argue that infamy emerges through simple melodramatic narratives casting CEOs as wrongdoers, whereas celebrity involves more complex dramatized narratives portraying CEOs as saviors. Focusing on CEOs’ liberal sociopolitical activism—a visible, ideologically-charged action that departs from conventional executive roles—we theorize that this behavior generates divergent constructions in partisan media: infamy in conservative outlets and celebrity in liberal outlets. We further argue that activism more readily generates infamy than celebrity because melodramatic narratives are simpler to construct and negative deviance is more readily perceived than positive deviance. We examine two moderators of these relationships. Firm performance differentially shapes these constructions, with poorer performance intensifying conservative-media infamy and stronger performance amplifying liberal-media celebrity. CEO social media engagement, conversely, attenuates both by constraining traditional media’s narrative discretion and reducing activism’s newsworthiness. We develop an LLM-based annotation system capturing CEO-directed sentiment, role attributions, and dramaturgical narratives in media articles. Analyzing 91,608 articles covering 705 S&P 500 CEOs across 45 ideologically polarized U.S. media outlets between 2016 and 2022, we find broad support for our hypotheses across our main and extensive supplemental analyses. Our findings advance understanding of CEO infamy and social evaluations more generally by revealing how partisan media construct divergent social evaluations of the same executive behavior through distinct narrative processes.

title: Can Voluntary Corporate Transparency Curb Corruption? Community-Level Evidence from Oil and Gas Fields in Africa
abstract: Voluntary corporate transparency seeks to promote accountability through disclosure, but substantive reporting does not by itself guarantee societal benefits. We examine whether this form of self-regulation can help curb corruption where formal oversight is weak, focusing on corporate support for the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (EITI), a multistakeholder initiative that promotes disclosure of company payments to host governments. We link geolocated data on African oil and gas fields and their operators to Afrobarometer surveys and satellite nighttime-light measures and estimate difference-in-differences models that track changes in outcomes around the same fields before and after operators endorse the EITI. We find that corporate EITI support is associated with lower perceived corruption and less reported bribery, greater civic engagement, greater perceived freedom to speak, and higher nighttime-light intensity, a proxy for local economic activity. The association with lower perceived corruption is stronger around fields with nearby NGO or aid-project activity, among residents living closer to fields, and among frequent users of traditional news media. Supplementary analyses provide indirect evidence that supporting firms were more transparent before mandatory disclosure laws took effect, and show that they had fewer joint-venture partners and larger ownership stakes after endorsement. Archival cases from Nigeria and Ghana illustrate how civil-society organizations and journalists use extractive-industry information to question firms and public authorities. The findings point to local governance benefits of voluntary transparency commitments and are consistent with an information-to-accountability account in which these benefits depend on both substantive reporting and local opportunities to scrutinize and use the information.

title: How Firms Respond to Carbon Taxation
abstract: Although environmental regulations can incentivize firms to reduce emissions, how firms adapt may depend not only on their organizational characteristics but also on the physical realities of their assets. This paper examines how multinational spread, an organizational feature in which firms own and manage similar production activities across countries, and the physical asset characteristics of production facilities jointly shape firms’ responses to carbon taxation. Using global, real-time satellite data on carbon emissions from 882 steel plants across 67 countries over 96 months (January 2015 to December 2022), we analyze operational adjustments firms can make to reduce carbon emissions: producing more cleanly by reducing emissions intensity of production or producing less by reducing asset utilization. We first examine how firms adapt to Canada’s carbon tax using a difference-in-differences (DID) design and then examine the impact of carbon taxes across countries using a stacked DID design. Our analysis reveals that, following Canada’s carbon tax, firms without multinational spread reduce carbon emissions primarily by lowering asset utilization; in contrast, firms with multinational spread additionally reduce emissions intensity of production. Importantly, our analysis of carbon taxes across countries shows that multinational spread alone does not dictate firm adaptation. Adaptation is fundamentally influenced by the physical technology on the ground: firms with multinational spread reduce emissions intensity of production and increase asset utilization at their clean (electric arc furnace) plants relative to dirty plants. Our study thus sheds light on how firms pursue different adaptation strategies at production facilities in response to carbon taxation.

title: The Emergence of Psychological Safety or its Mirage
abstract: Leaders often strive to foster psychological safety in teams, and yet it may not emerge. This study builds grounded theory on how psychological safety emerges, or not, on teams. We draw on longitudinal ethnographic data from a matched pair case study of two teams over two years, including verbatim meeting transcripts that elicit the micro-processes affecting psychological safety and interviews that elucidate team members’ interpretations. We identify an illusion initially present on both teams in which surface markers of psychological safety existed but team members nonetheless continued to avoid interpersonal risk—what we call a psychological safety mirage. This occurred because external pressures on leaders spurred them to take self-protective actions that inadvertently reinforced interpersonal risk, despite their continued efforts to invite contributions. One team was eventually able to break from this mirage through a three-phase de-risking process that facilitated psychological safety emergence: (1) collectively recognizing the underlying risk faced by team members, (2) de-risking contributions by offering opportunities to build skills, through which safety was demonstrated and reinforced, and (3) enacting psychological safety, with all team members contributing, reinforcing, and sharing in the benefits of reduced interpersonal risk. This paper advances theory on psychological safety by conceptualizing a team-level de-risking process model that facilitates its emergence and by characterizing its mirage.

title: The Digital Journey of Health Insurance Marketing: Narrative Ads and Product Page Design
abstract: Selling health insurance through digital advertising is fundamentally different from selling most consumer products online: health insurance protects against abstract future risks, and regulatory constraints prohibit transactions from closing on third-party platforms, forcing consumers to transition from the ad platform to the insurer’s own product page. We examine how aligning narrative ad content with product page design sustains persuasion across this mandatory handoff. In a randomized field experiment with a leading Chinese insurer on Douyin, we study 335 ads that generated nearly 17 million impressions and 777,412 click-throughs. Users who clicked were randomly routed to either a fact-based product page or one incorporating a customer experience exemplar. Purchase conversion rises most when narrative ads are paired with the exemplar page, increasing from 1.51% to 2.05%, implying roughly 8,400 additional policies per month at campaign scale. Neither element is effective in isolation. A causal mediation analysis confirms that sustained engagement on the product page accounts for more than 80% of the total effect. To address algorithm-driven selection in ad delivery and self-selection into clicking, we employ a sequential endogeneity correction strategy and confirm robustness with causal forests. Aligning ad design with product page design significantly improves conversion in regulated digital markets. History: Catherine Tucker served as the senior editor. Funding: X.
