The Search for Parental Leave and the Early-Career Gender Wage Gap
abstract: Gender differences in preferences for parental leave contribute to the early-career growth in the gender wage gap among highly educated millennial Americans. Estimating a hedonic job-search model, I show that, while both men and women experience wage growth by entering firms offering better pay and benefits, the wage gap increases as women accept lower wages upon receiving job offers from employers providing parental leave. The wage-gap growth could decline by 60% if preferences for paid parental leave did not differ by gender. It could also decline if mandating and subsidizing the provision of paid leave muted workers’ leave-wage trade-off.

title: Getting Teachers Back to Study: Input-Based Teacher Incentives and Student Achievement
abstract: Rewarding teachers on the basis of student performance is a growing trend in educational policy. This paper estimates the effects of a policy that ties payments with teachers’ pedagogical skills instead. We study a large-scale reform in Chile that introduced financial incentives tied to a teacher evaluation system. Using a unique administrative data set of over 500, 000 student-teacher-year matches, we estimate the effect of the policy on student performance exploiting the program’s gradual roll-out through a differences-in-differences analysis. We document precise, null effects of the policy on student math and language standardized test scores. Estimating a structural model of teacher skills and student performance, we show that by making incentives more homogeneous across the distribution of teacher characteristics policymakers can improve the policy’s effects on student performance and overall welfare.

title: A new equilibrium: COVID-19 lockdowns and WFH persistence
abstract: This paper documents a robust link between COVID-19 lockdowns and the uptake and persistence of working from home (WFH) practices. Exploiting rich longitudinal data, we use a difference-in-differences strategy to compare office workers in three heavily locked-down Australian states to similar workers in less affected states. Locked-down workers sustain 43% higher WFH levels through 2023  0.5 days per week  with a monotonic doseresponse relationship. Persistence is driven by adjustments on both sides of the labor market: employers downsize office space and open remote/hybrid positions, while employees relocate away from city centers and invest in home offices and technology.

title: Immigration, Local Crowd-Out and Labor Market Effects
Heterogeneous Passthrough from TFP to Wages
Incentive Effects of Disability Benefits
Understanding the Heterogeneity of Earnings Losses After Job Displacement: A Machine Learning Approach
Structural Empirical Analysis of Vacancy Referrals with Imperfect Monitoring and the Strategic Use of Sickness Absence
abstract: This paper provides a structural analysis of the role of job vacancy referrals (VRs) by public employment agencies in the job search behavior of unemployed individuals, incorporating institutional features of the monitoring of search behavior by the agencies. Notably, rejections of VRs may lead to sanctions (temporary benefits reductions) while workers may report sick to avoid those. We estimate models using German administrative data from social security records linked with caseworker recorded data on VRs, sick reporting and sanctions. The analysis highlights the influence of aspects of the health care system on unemployment durations. We estimate that for around 25% of unemployed workers, removing the channel that enables strategic sick reporting reduces the mean unemployment duration by 4 days.

title: Living for the lineage: Ancestral beliefs and the spiritual foundations of fertility in Sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: Conventional demographic models systematically overestimate fertility decline in sub-Saharan Africa. This paper proposes a complementary explanation grounded in a prevalent but understudied belief system: ancestors influence the living and seek the continuation of their lineage. In this worldview, having children becomes a moral and collective duty, rooted in the spiritual responsibility to ensure the survival of the lineage. Drawing on first-hand data, novel ethnographic information, and historical and contemporary surveys, I document a strong and quantitatively large positive relationship between ancestral beliefs and fertility across contexts and time periods. A simple model in which children are a public good for the lineage rationalizes the patterns observed in the data: the fertility effect of ancestral beliefs is concentrated in patrilineal societies, and a specific form of free-riding emerges among siblings whose children continue the same family line. • Beliefs in ancestral spirits raise fertility across sub-Saharan Africa. • Shown in Benin, the DR Congo, 19 countries today, and global folklore records. • Having children is a collective duty to the lineage, not a private choice. • Effects concentrate in patrilineal societies, where sons continue the line. • Free-riding appears among siblings whose children continue the same line.

title: Comment on “Slackness, Openness, and the Anatomy of Cash Transfer Multipliers” by Minki Kim and Mitchell VanVuren
Fiscal cyclicality and the information channel of government spending shocks
Emotional State and Market Activity: Cause or Consequence?
abstract: Abstract Many observers have asserted that there is a correlation between traders’ emotional states and asset market behaviour, with Joviality associated with high prices and Fear with low prices. In this paper, we conduct a laboratory experiment to examine the direction of causality in this relationship. The results show that moods, induced by videos, shown in virtual reality, do not influence market prices. However, there is a strong relationship between market activity and subsequent emotional states, suggesting that the correlation between emotional state and market activity is driven by the influence of market activity on emotional state, not the other way around.

title: Human Capital as a Driver of Automation: Theory and Evidence From China's College Expansion
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies how human capital shapes both the level and direction of automation. We develop an endogenous Schumpeterian growth model in which skilled labor is allocated across production, horizontal automation of new tasks, and vertical upgrading of existing automated tasks. A positive skilled‐labor shock reallocates labor toward R&D and accelerates automation along both margins. Using China's 1999 college enrollment expansion as a natural experiment, we find that firms in skill‐intensive industries increased robot adoption significantly more after the reform, with a stronger effect on the horizontal than the vertical margin.

title: Beyond external pressure: how management technical proficiency and financial slack shape hospitals' response to environmental regulation
Synergistic policy intervention for green investment and bond pricing: An optimization framework with carbon credits and subsidies
Corporate reporting under the EU taxonomy framework: a sectoral and geographical analysis of eligibility and alignment
Energy inequality and deforestation in developing countries
A latent regional greenhouse gas emissions index for Ukraine's energy sector: Insights from a MIMIC model
Feed-in-Tariff with unexpected emission rebound? Incomplete carbon pricing and inter-fuel substitution in manufacturing
Key factors, commercialization models, and effectiveness of policy tools for vehicle-to-grid integration in China: a study based on asymmetric evolutionary game approach
Product scope, product switching, and ownership structure
Impact of embedded leverage on trading activity in spot, options, and futures markets
An Investigation of Market Invariance for the Tokyo Stock Exchange
abstract: ABSTRACT We test the invariance‐of‐bet hypothesis from Kyle and Obizhaeva (2016) for the Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE). The pooled regression coefficients of the logarithm of the number of trades on the logarithm of the product of volume and volatility range from 0.663 to 0.665, close to the theoretical value of two‐thirds predicted by the invariance‐of‐bet hypothesis. Using the TSE as a relatively clean benchmark, we further examine when the empirical two‐thirds relation deviates from its theoretical prediction. We find that deviations become more pronounced during extreme market conditions, for stocks facing more binding tick‐size constraints, and around the market open and close. Our results also suggest that measurement errors in transaction data can contribute to deviations from the two‐thirds relation.

title: Misperceiving the roots of inequality: Cross-country evidence from Europe
Solution method of a macroeconomic model with rational expectations
Pro-poor land reforms, education and fertility: international evidence, 1820-2010
abstract: Abstract Land reforms are often assumed to promote economic development in unequal societies. However, supportive cross-country evidence remains limited, largely because major land reforms are rare events that provide insufficient identifying variation in small samples. Drawing on a global dataset of major land reforms over the period 1820–2010, we provide evidence that pro-poor land reforms promote economic development by increasing school enrollment and reducing fertility, whereas non-pro-poor land reforms do not. We further show that these empirical patterns are consistent with the relaxation of credit constraints among poor households and the weakening of the political power of the landed elites, which together facilitate greater human capital investment and demographic transition. Event-study analyses, semi-parametric difference-in-differences estimations, two-way fixed effects, instrumental variable estimates, and placebo tests collectively suggest that the results are not driven by endogeneity.

title: Resource nationalism and economic outcomes: evidence from national policy interventions
The effect of being a poll worker on democratic attitudes in a post-conflict society: evidence from an experiment in Colombia
abstract: This paper examines how citizens’ direct participation in democratic processes boosts attitudes toward democratic practices. Focusing on compulsory poll working, we argue that citizens selected to work at polling stations on Election Day gain additional information about democratic procedures, and that this shapes their attitudes toward electoral integrity and democracy. We test our claims by leveraging a pre-registered large-scale experiment from the 2023 Colombian regional elections. Based on a unique survey dataset of over 25,000 poll workers matched with a sample of ordinary citizens, we identify a positive and robust causal effect of electoral task management on attitudes toward electoral integrity and democracy that operates mainly via a theory-based mechanism, but also via a practice-based mechanism. Moreover, we discover that this treatment effect is smaller in municipalities heavily affected by political violence during previous civil conflict.

title: Economic dynamics of flood damage: The roles of private capital, public capital, and financial accelerator
Disparities in climate risk-mitigation and recreation services in Grenoble (France)
abstract: Summary Urban green spaces provide cultural and climate risk-mitigation ecosystem services (ES) critical for the well-being of urban residents. Yet these benefits are not equally shared across social groups, and environmental segregation - i.e., the spatial separation of population groups between areas of contrasted environmental quality - is common. For instance, environmental justice studies have shown that green space acreage and quality are typically lower in low-income neighbourhoods. However, more detailed assessments integrating a range of ES and the diverse needs of multiple groups are needed to effectively inform equitable urban planning. Here, we combine socio-demographic spatial data with ES modelling to assess social disparities in the distribution of three ES - heatwave mitigation, flood regulation, and urban recreation - in the Grenoble metropolitan area, France. Our results show that low-income households generally benefit from lower climate risk mitigation, but from equal or slightly greater urban recreation opportunities. We also identify mismatches between ES supply and demand from vulnerable groups, which are particularly acute in disadvantaged neighborhoods. These findings highlight the importance of integrating social needs and vulnerabilities into urban greening strategies. Policies that move beyond generic measures of green space provision and explicitly consider multiple ES can help ensure that urban green infrastructure delivers fair and effective benefits across diverse communities.

title: A post-growth deal for Italy: Exploring the coalition-building potential of non-reformist reforms
abstract: Challenging green growth narratives, degrowth argues that achieving ecological sustainability in high-income countries requires a democratically planned and socially just downscaling of production and consumption, alongside a reorientation of economic institutions toward collective wellbeing within planetary boundaries. While post-growth and degrowth scholarship has increasingly shifted from critique to policy proposals, limited attention has been paid to the political agency and coalition-building capacity required to implement such policies. This paper asks whether a post-growth policy package can function as an emancipatory tool for building a counter-hegemonic alliance capable of contesting growth-dependent capitalism. We examine perceptions of a “Post-Growth Deal” composed of five non-reformist reforms – Universal Care Income, Universal Public Services, Working Time Reduction, a Public Job Guarantee, and Deliberative Forums – among three strategically positioned actor groups: environmental activists, labor union members, and progressive political party members. Using a mixed-methods approach that combines focus group discussions with a survey, we analyze the desirability, communicability, achievability, and perceived popularity of these measures. Our findings show that work-centered policies, particularly Working Time Reduction and a Green Job Guarantee, display the strongest potential for cross-group alignment, while more redistributive and participatory measures face greater ideological and communicative barriers. The study contributes to ecological economics by empirically assessing the coalition-building potential of post-growth policies, foregrounding compromise and political strategy, and situating degrowth debates within a southern European context, by focussing on the case-study of Italy.

title: ESG performance, tone of earnings calls, and market reaction during an economic crisis
abstract: Abstract This study explores the relationship between firms’ environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance, the tone of earnings calls, and market reaction during the COVID-19 outbreak. Using a comprehensive sample of European listed firms and a robust methodology, our findings show a less optimistic tone of the earnings calls during COVID-19 and a negative relationship between ESG and tone, wherein firms with lower ESG project a more positive outlook in their earnings calls to reassure stakeholders. We find a positive market reaction to the tone of earnings calls, which is more pronounced for firms that seek to reassure with an inflated tone, even in presence of lower ESG. This study offers new evidence on the value relevance of non-financial information as a driver of managerial tone and the effectiveness of companies’ communication strategies in reassuring stakeholders and market participants during an economic crisis; it provides insights into how companies could respond to manage stakeholders’ expectations when dealing with significant large-scale disruptions.

title: Insurer Capital and Organizational Forms in Market Equilibrium
abstract: Abstract We explain the coexistence of stock and mutual organizational forms and their relative dominance in different insurance markets in a market equilibrium model. Organizational forms endogenously reflect the benefits and costs of equity and the impact of insurer operating efficiencies. Stock insurers are larger and more efficient than mutual insurers. Mutualization (i) increases with taxes and agency costs, (ii) decreases with the mean and idiosyncratic variability of insuree losses, (iii) increases with aggregate insurer asset and liability risks, and (iv) increases (decreases) with the market return when insuree loss variance is low (high). Evidence from U.S. insurance data supports all our predictions. (JEL G12, G22, G32)

title: Industry relatedness and technological diversification across patent applicants: evidence from Brazil
Climate Change and Agricultural Export Margins: The Role of Financial Development
Forward-Looking Disclosures and Corporate Innovation: Evidence from Chinese Listed Firms
Digital Governance and Firm-Level Labor Income Share: Evidence from China’s Government Services Pilot Reform
Toward a Behavioral–Institutional Framework of Socially Responsible Investment Adoption: A Bibliometric Review and Research Agenda
abstract: ABSTRACT The growing prominence of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) considerations has increased scholarly and market attention to socially responsible investment (SRI) as an approach that combines financial and sustainability considerations. This study examines the development, intellectual structure, and determinants of SRI adoption through an integrated bibliometric analysis, systematic literature review, and thematic analysis. This study analyses Scopus‐indexed publications from 2015 to 2026; it combines bibliometric mapping of 358 documents with a systematic synthesis of 72 eligible studies. The findings indicate substantial growth in SRI research, particularly in recent years, alongside increasing thematic attention to investor behavior, sustainability, ESG, and responsible investment. The systematic review identifies 13 recurring determinants associated with SRI adoption, organized through thematic analysis into five themes: psychological and Behavioral; social, moral and sustainability; knowledge and literacy; financial and risk; and institutional. Building on these themes, the study proposes a Behavioral–institutional framework in which the four individual‐level themes serve as antecedents of SRI intention and adoption, while government policy support acts as a contextual moderator of the intention–adoption relationship. The framework is presented as a conceptual synthesis, with its relationships offered as propositions for future empirical testing. The study offers directions for future research and suggests possible implications for policymakers, financial institutions, and investment practitioners.

title: Measuring digital technology adoption: a multidimensional scale development and validation
abstract: Existing research widely acknowledges the significant effects of digitalisation, yet empirical work often treats it as a unified construct, which obscures its underlying technological diversity. This paper addresses that limitation by developing a psychometrically validated scale of digital technology adoption that captures the multidimensional and functionally distinct nature of digital technologies. Drawing on theoretical insights from innovation studies and digital technology research, we identify four core dimensions that structure firms’ adoption profiles: digital communication technology, digital in situ technology, digital data analytics technology, and digital networking technology. We develop and validate a 19-item scale that operationalises these dimensions and reflects the different coordination, optimisation, data access, and location access functions that digital technologies perform. The resulting measurement instrument offers scholars a more precise means to examine how digital technologies shape organisational processes. It also provides managers with a diagnostic tool for assessing adoption patterns and guiding technology investment decisions.

title: The price of a nation: The effects of financial incentives on support for union in Scotland
A Blessing in Disguise: The Long‐Term Effects of Childhood Exposure to the Boll Weevil on Old‐Age Male Longevity
abstract: The infamous agricultural pest, the boll weevil, spread across southern US counties between 1892 and 1920. It had devastating impacts on cotton production, a highly child-labor-intensive crop. This study examines how the arrival of the boll weevil and the subsequent reductions in child labor affect later-life mortality outcomes. Using Social Security Administration death records linked with the 1940 census, we document that the staggered spread of the boll weevil improved the longevity of exposed male children. Full exposure to the boll weevil is associated with an intent-to-treat effect of 1-3 months of higher longevity. We show that the estimated effects are robust across a wide array of specifications, are not driven by sociodemographic and socioeconomic compositional change in the final sample, and are not associated with pre-existing trends in the outcome. Further, we find larger impacts among Blacks, children of lower educated mothers, whose fathers work in the farming industry, and those born in high cotton intensity counties. Moreover, the effects appear to be substantially larger among children in states with less restrictive child labor policies, implying the role of these policies in reducing the adverse effects of child labor in the absence of the boll weevil in cotton production counties. Affected children are more likely to migrate, and their destination counties are more likely to be urban and have higher socioeconomic scores. The 1940 census suggests that the exposed children attain higher levels of education and have higher socioeconomic scores. We discuss the policy implications of these results in relation to child labor and school attendance policies in developing countries.

title: Not in Isolation: The Influence of Patient‐Sharing Networks on Psychotropic Prescribing for People With Dementia
abstract: The use of low-value care practices is extensive. Clinical guidelines and alignment in prescribing practice can facilitate a reduction in related medical practices by physicians as part of de-implementation strategies. Peer influence within physicians' networks can significantly impact clinical behaviors, including the adoption or abandonment of certain prescribing practices. We examine the physicians prescribing alignment related to de-implementing low-value psychotropics prescribing to people with dementia. Using Finnish prescription register data (2014-2020), we identified patient-sharing networks and applied instrumental variable estimation to account for reflection and endogeneity. We instrument patient-sharing network prescribing using peers' peers' prescribing behavior-physicians who share patients with a focal physician's peers but not with the focal physician themselves-to isolate peer effects on psychotropic prescribing to dementia patients. We found that a one percentage point higher share of psychotropic prescribing within physicians' patient-sharing network was associated with a 1.5 percentage point increase in the physician's psychotropic prescribing when controls and time-invariant physician characteristics were fixed. Our findings underscore the need for consensus among physicians to facilitate the de-implementation of low-value care in the context of dementia care.

title: Dangerous Liaisons? Debt Supply and Convenience Yield Spillovers in the Euro Area*
abstract: Abstract The literature established that a sovereign bond’s “convenience yield” premium diminishes when that country issues more debt. But how is this convenience yield affected when another country issues sovereign debt? Using high-frequency identification and debt management offices’ communication, we find that an increase in German or French debt reduces convenience yields across the eurozone. Spillovers to low-risk countries are one-for-one while those to riskier countries are smaller. To rationalize these findings, we develop a model with heterogeneous credit risk. Safe sovereign bonds are close substitutes to hedge against idiosyncratic risk, explaining large spillovers, while risky bonds are poor substitutes.

title: Pay incentives to run for local governments
abstract: Local governments in advanced democracies have increasingly struggled to attract political candidates, weakening electoral competition and accountability at the municipal level. While several factors may contribute to this trend, politicians’ salaries represent one of the few policy levers that can be directly adjusted by policymakers. We study a large-scale reform that substantially increased local politicians’ pay, exploiting quasi-experimental variation in election timing across municipalities. On average, we find no evidence that higher salaries increase political entry. Instead, the effects are concentrated in specific local contexts: municipalities with lower entry barriers and less affluent areas experience an increase in candidacies, particularly among first-time candidates. In the poorest areas, the reform further alters the composition of local political elites, shifting recruitment toward candidates with different educational and occupational backgrounds.

title: EXPRESS: How Gig Sellers Do the Hustle
abstract: We conceptualize and develop theoretical insights related to a neglected category of market actors: gig sellers. Gig sellers are independent agents who sell products on behalf of a specific brand with marketing support. They face semi-entrepreneurial opportunities, meaning that while they are entirely responsible for managing the customer sales funnel, they do not develop new products or services like conventional entrepreneurs. They are compensated solely by sales commissions and do not receive salaries or benefits like organizational salesreps. Drawing on a large set of qualitative data from effective agents, we inductively and abductively draw inspiration both from literature and our analyses to unpack how these agents seize the opportunity to accomplish what is important to them. We find prominent reliance on effectual versus predictive practices is crucial to satisfactory achievement of outcomes. We expand our understanding of the range of outcomes that gig selling may result in, whether it be to remain in gig sales (enacting long-term loyalty, switching teams, or enriching) or enter alternative opportunity corridors (pursuing entrepreneurship, seeking employment). Our theoretical insights contrast with findings regarding salespeople in institutional settings and other categories of independent agents. Practical implications for agents and organizations are developed.

title: Government‐funded experimentation: How startups use R&D contracts to resolve uncertainty
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Startups use experimentation to reduce technological and market uncertainty, but experimentation is costly and unevenly funded. This paper examines how government‐funded experimentation relates to subsequent performance among high‐tech startups that receive federal awards. Using data on $32 billion in US government R&D contracts awarded to high‐tech startups between 2001 and 2018, I distinguish between technology experimentation, measured by the value of R&D contracts, and market experimentation, measured by the number of agencies awarding the R&D contracts. Market experimentation is positively associated with subsequent employment, sales, and acquisition, while technology experimentation shows weaker associations with these outcomes. The findings are consistent with startups using information from multiple government buyers to learn about market opportunities and improve subsequent performance. Managerial Summary High‐tech startups need to test both whether their technology works and where demand exists, but venture capital often leaves this experimentation unfunded. Using data on $32 billion in US government R&D contracts awarded to high‐tech startups from 2001 to 2018, this paper shows that startups funded by more government agencies subsequently have higher employment and sales and are more likely to be acquired. Larger R&D contract amounts have less consistent relationships with these outcomes. For managers, the findings suggest considering what different government customers can help the firm learn. For policymakers, they suggest that the diversity of a startup's public customer base is a vital margin to consider alongside the overall size of its R&D awards.

title: EXPRESS: Slim Shading in Ad Auctions: Adjustment of Bidding Strategies to First-Price Rules
abstract: We study how bidders adjusted to a switch from second-price to first-price auction rules on a large online advertising exchange. Under first-price rules, bidders should strategically reduce (“shade”) their bids. To assess whether observed bid reductions were sufficient given the competition each bidder faced, we develop a nonparametric estimator of a lower bound on the valuation underlying each bid. The estimator relies on localized measures of competition and does not require assumptions of bidder symmetry, valuation independence, or equilibrium bidding. Applying the method to more than 40 million auctions involving eight major demand-side platforms, we find pervasive insufficient bid shading after the switch. The implied lower bounds on valuations remain substantially above pre-switch levels for at least three months after the transition, indicating that none of the bidders we study shaded sufficiently. This finding is robust to alternative definitions of local competition, richer conditioning information, and variations in the assumptions underlying the estimator. The results suggest that adjustment to major auction-design changes can be surprisingly slow even among sophisticated algorithmic bidders, with implications for marketplace design and the interpretation of short-run “A/B test” experiments.

title: Advertising by Recruiting Influencers
Whiplash: Congestion Dissipation in a Disrupted Circulatory Shipping System
abstract: The (post)pandemic period was marked by numerous port disruptions, leading to delays and rising costs for shippers. We build a fluid model in transient states to investigate how a disruption at one port can affect the disrupted port and its counterpart in another country in a circulatory container shipping system, where a stream of fleets moves goods back and forth between the two ports. Port disruption leads to two types of congestion: the inbound backlogs, which occur when ships are unable to enter the port, and the outbound backlogs, which arise when goods are unable to be loaded onto ships for transport to other ports. We analytically characterize the system’s recovery time, measured from the onset of the port closure until normal operations are restored, and the dynamics of inbound and outbound backlogs during recovery. We identify a whiplash effect in which outbound backlogs alternate between ports, creating oscillatory congestion patterns because of the disruption-induced uneven spatial distribution of ships. Our analysis reveals that simply increasing ship capacity may not expedite system recovery, highlighting the importance of coordination between port authorities and shipping companies when jointly planning capacity expansions. Furthermore, we examine several extensions of the model. We use the two-port system as a building block to analyze bipartite and cyclic network structures, and we also consider scenarios in which a port experiences multiple disruptions. In all cases, the whiplash effect persists, thereby demonstrating the robustness of our findings. Finally, we use our theory model prediction as a feature and apply machine learning techniques to predict the time that vessels spend in Shanghai Port after a typhoon disruption and show that using our model predictor, alongside all relevant vessel and voyage attributes as raw features, significantly reduces prediction errors by 10%–30% on average compared with not using it. This paper was accepted by Elena Katok, operations management. Funding: This work was supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada [Grant RGPIN-2021-04295]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05427 .

title: Biodiversity Risk in the Corporate Bond Market
abstract: We show that a biodiversity risk premium has emerged in the U.S. corporate bond market following the United Nations Biodiversity Conference (COP15) in October 2021. COP15 placed biodiversity on the global regulatory agenda and raised transition risks for exposed firms. After COP15, a one standard deviation increase in a firm’s biodiversity footprint is associated with a 7% increase in its secondary market yield spreads, whereas this relation is insignificant before COP15. The biodiversity effect is also present in primary bond markets, most pronounced for medium-term bonds and distinct from climate-related mechanisms. Furthermore, a higher biodiversity footprint is associated with a lower likelihood of issuing medium-term bonds after COP15, consistent with firms managing their biodiversity-related risks. Evidence from firms’ biodiversity dependencies suggests that physical biodiversity risks are also priced in the bond market. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07660 .

title: Do Fund Managers’ Commitments to Responsible Investing Affect Private Information Acquisition, Information Environment, and Corporate Sustainability?
abstract: We investigate the effects of mutual funds’ commitments to responsible investing on their information acquisition activities and the corresponding externalities for other stakeholders. After committing to responsible investing (via United Nations Principles for Responsible Investment (UNPRI)), fund managers increase private information acquisition activities, that is, corporate site visits, particularly focusing on environmental and social issues. These visits generate negligible private investment value for the visiting funds. However, the information environment at the stock level improves following these visits with lower consensus analyst forecast errors. In addition to the information production role of these visits, they also generate positive externalities for other stakeholders through incremental improvements in the sustainability practices of the firms receiving sustainability-focused site visits from UNPRI fund managers. Collectively, the paper highlights the private costs and social benefits of responsible investing. This paper was accepted by Will Cong, finance. Funding: S. Agarwal and J. Sulaeman acknowledge research support from Sustainable and Green Finance Institute [Grant WBS A-0006413-00-00]. Y. Zhang acknowledges financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72402239] and China Scholarship Council. This work was supported by the Ministry of Education, Singapore [Social Science and Humanities Research Thematic Grant SSRC2024-SSHRTG-022]. Any opinions, findings and conclusions or recommendations expressed in this material are those of the author(s) and do not reflect the views of the Social Science Research Council (Singapore) and the Ministry of Education (Singapore). Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08443 .

title: When Data Scientists Meet Domain Experts: Artificial Intelligence, Epistemic Conflict, and Knowledge Transformation
abstract: Predictive AI models developed by data scientists promise to transform organizational knowledge, yet in practice the predictions remain inscrutable to domain experts. Existing explanations situate the problems in the opacity of the AI tools, failed adoption, or jurisdictional conflict, but offer limited insight into how to make the knowledge accessible. Here we show how the problem emerges from the competing epistemic stances of data scientists and domain experts, which create conflict over how to produce and evaluate knowledge. We then ask how data scientists and domain experts address that conflict so that their work with AI satisfies each group’s standards for producing and evaluating knowledge. Drawing on an 18-month inductive study of three large Indian banks, we show that the data scientists produce new knowledge, but domain experts hold the power to decide whether it is deployed. Our findings distinguish between epistemic and jurisdictional conflict. We show that data scientists first try to address the epistemic conflict directly through assimilative practices that follow one epistemic stance or the other. When these practices fail to transform knowledge, data scientists learn to address the conflict indirectly through four bridging practices. These practices help the domain experts transform knowledge by embedding the data scientists’ predictions in the boundary objects and practices that the domain experts already use. Our findings reveal how power based on expertise rather than jurisdictional control can make possible the coproduction of knowledge.

title: When meaningful work becomes inaccessible: Disability, ableism and passive agency
abstract: Why does meaningful work become inaccessible to certain groups? Existing literature increasingly recognizes that access to meaningful work is shaped by both subjective experiences and objective conditions, yet it remains less clear about how and why such access becomes systematically constrained. In particular, prior studies tend to foreground workers’ active agency in engaging with, negotiating or resisting these conditions of meaningful work, but they offer limited insight into how this capacity itself may be restricted. Drawing on Archer’s distinction between active and passive agency, we conceptualize passive agency as a mechanism through which structural constraints limit workers’ capability for purposive action. Based on 33 interviews with disabled workers in China, we show how ableism acts as a structural constraint, positioning disabled workers as passive agents, restricting their capacity to experience work as meaningful by limiting opportunities for autonomy, dignity and recognition. In doing so, we extend current understanding of meaningful work by specifying how structural constraints give rise to passive agency, thereby systematically foreclosing access to meaningful work. We also clarify contingent conditions under which more active forms of agency may be enacted, and thus meaningful work can be sustained.

title: Unethical Leadership and Employee Creative Unethicality—Do Dark Personalities Matter?
abstract: Abstract Recent research has shown that employee creativity may also be unethical; however, our understanding of such behaviour is limited. Existing literature suggests that certain leadership behaviours foster creativity; hence, employee creative unethicality may be similarly underpinned by unethical leadership—that is, leadership that rejects accepted norms. Building on the focus‐strand logic of self‐regulation theory, we argue that the degree of unethical leadership has an inverted U‐shaped relationship with employee creative unethicality, and that this relationship is conditional on employee Dark Triad personality traits. A time‐lagged survey of 468 employees from 26 firms in Bangladesh, India and Malaysia confirms the hypothesized inverted U‐shaped effect and finds that this relationship is positively moderated by employee Machiavellianism and psychopathy. The findings contribute to understanding when creative unethicality escalates within organizations by showing that unethical leadership does not invariably translate into employee creative unethicality. Under high unethical leadership, employees guided by self‐regulation may instead pursue more ethical solutions. However, when employees possess Machiavellian or psychopathic traits, their self‐regulatory tendencies are compromised, thereby increasing the likelihood of creative unethicality under unethical leadership.

title: From Biospheric Values to Employees' Green Supply Chain Engagement: The Dual Mediating Roles of Generative Concern and Environmental Attitude
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper asks how employees' biospheric values translate into engagement with their organization's green supply chain practices, and why some employees act on those values more readily than others. Although environmental attitude is a well‐established predictor of pro‐environmental engagement, the motivational role of generative concern, the disposition to contribute beyond oneself to future generations, has received limited attention. Framed by the natural‐resource‐based view and drawing on Value‐Belief‐Norm theory, the study develops and tests a moderated‐mediation model in which biospheric values relate to employees' perceived green supply chain engagement through the parallel mediating roles of generative concern and environmental attitude, with generative leadership as an enabling condition. Data were collected through purposive, department‐stratified sampling from employees across nine public‐sector departments in Pakistan and analyzed with partial least squares structural equation modeling, complemented by an artificial neural network analysis as a predictive robustness check. Biospheric values were positively associated with perceived green supply chain engagement, both directly and through generative concern and environmental attitude, operating as distinct parallel mediators. Generative concern remained a significant predictor alongside the established value‐to‐attitude pathway, and generative leadership strengthened the value‐driven pathways while showing no direct association, consistent with a contextual‐enabler role. Discriminant validity and full collinearity checks supported construct distinctness and reduced common‐method‐bias concerns. By positioning generative concern as an underexamined motivational driver of sustainability engagement, the paper offers a focused extension of value‐based environmental research, points to a possible micro‐foundation of green organizational capability, and offers practical guidance for strengthening employee sustainability engagement in public‐sector organizations.

title: Extending the Strategy Tripod View to Explain Circular Economy Implementation in SMEs: A Systematic Review
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how interorganisational arrangements shape circular economy ( CE ) implementation in small‐ and medium‐sized enterprises (SMEs). Existing research identifies resource‐, institution‐ and industry‐related influences but insufficiently specifies how external arrangements condition their contribution to implementation. We systematically review 139 studies through the strategy tripod view's constituent perspectives and assess the strength of evidence supporting a system‐level extension. We develop circular value system architecture (CVSA), comprising connectivity, coordination locus and participation terms, and distinguish these attributes from resource access, deployment, capability augmentation and focal‐SME coordination burden. Seven proposition groups specify how arrangements may shape implementation across the three strategic paths. Along the resource path, deployment capability conditions the usefulness of external access, while coordination allocation shapes the SME's burden. Along the institutional path, environmental information exchange may condition the pressure–implementation relationship, depending on circular innovation orientation. Along the industry path, weaker bargaining positions may constrain implementation through less favourable participation terms. The framework identifies a participation tension: Resource shortages may increase SMEs' need for external complements while restricting their capacity to obtain and sustain them on viable terms. Material constraints further qualify which arrangements are useful. The review contributes by explaining how arrangements condition established strategic determinants, when external resources become operationally useful and why external provision may inadequately compensate for internal scarcity. The framework offers managers and policymakers a basis for diagnosing CE implementation constraints.

title: Structuring Firms' Alignment With the Sustainable Development Goals: ESG and Broader Corporate Performance Indicators
abstract: ABSTRACT The literature on ESG indicators highlights the relevance of corporate contributions to sustainable development. However, fragmentation and a lack of standardized indicators limit alignment between corporate performance and global sustainability goals. This study examines how the literature has addressed the relationship between Corporate Performance, the SDGs, and ESG indicators in recent years, identifying prevailing approaches, measurement strategies, and reported findings. We conduct a systematic literature review complemented by bibliometric and content analyses. Results suggest a marked increase in publications after 2019 and a predominance of governance indicators in studies linking ESG to corporate performance and the SDGs. Across the sample, more than 300 distinct ESG indicators are identified, evidencing heterogeneity in measurement practices. Based on these findings, we develop a conceptual framework that clarifies structural patterns in the ESG–SDG–Corporate nexus and contributes to greater conceptual integration in corporate sustainability research.

title: Are Supply Chain Relationships Characterised by Similar Carbon Policies? An Exploratory Study Using Social Network Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT The carbon footprint from manufacturing companies' supply chains presents significant opportunities for climate change mitigation. Supply chain emissions management is gaining increasing importance in the EU, where regulations target both firms' direct and supply chain impacts. Yet the consistency of carbon regulatory requirements across supply chains and their effects on business relationships remain unclear. This study uses empirical data to explore the association of similar national carbon regulations with the likelihood of observing a tie between two companies in undirected buyer–supplier networks. Using an exponential random graph model (ERGM) on 6027 firms and 11,483 edges, we assess whether companies under similar regulatory conditions are more likely to form undirected buyer–supplier ties. Results indicate that national carbon regulation simultaneously is associated with clustering among regulated firms and cross‐regulatory ties that can enable spillovers. Unregulated firms show weaker clustering, suggesting that even when national regulation is absent, firms remain indirectly exposed to decarbonisation requirements through their connections to regulated partners. Our findings advance sustainable supply chain management by demonstrating how regulatory homophily creates the network conditions through which coercive pressures originating from national carbon regulation may extend indirectly across international supply networks.

title: Double Materiality Assessment Profiles Under Institutional Pressure: Early Evidence From the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive
abstract: ABSTRACT Companies reporting under the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) identify required disclosures through a double materiality assessment (DMA)—a complex process for which no established practice existed in the first reporting years. Organizations facing such uncertainty are known to orient themselves toward practices prevalent in their institutional environment. While this phenomenon, institutional isomorphism, has been used to explain reporting practices and the design of materiality assessment processes, assessment results have not been studied. This study asks whether DMA profiles converge within the sectoral and national reference groups implied by mimetic and normative isomorphic pressure. DMA results are hand‐coded from CSRD‐compliant sustainability reports for the financial years (FY) 2024 and 2025 of 244 large listed EU firms, yielding 4697 decisions at the reporting‐standard level and 18,040 at the impact, risk, and opportunity (IRO) dimension level. These profiles are analyzed using logistic regressions, linear probability models, and permutation tests on pairwise profile distances. Firms' DMA profiles are more similar to those of their sector and country peers than to the remaining sample. Between years, which reporting standards a firm assesses as material converges only within sectors. At the IRO‐dimension level, convergence is observed for both reference groups, but only for the impact materiality half of the profiles. Institutional pressure is thus associated with the topics firms report and with how they frame impacts related to such topics, but not with how they frame risks and opportunities.

title: Financial Innovation for Sustainable Development: The Mediating Role of Green Credit in Advancing Human Well‐Being
abstract: ABSTRACT This research investigates the links between traditional and digital financial inclusion, green credit and selected dimensions of human well‐being across 32 high‐ and upper‐middle‐income nations from 2011 until 2020. Two‐step system GMM models are used to investigate infant mortality, life expectancy and undernourishment, supplemented by a principal‐component‐based well‐being index. Commercial bank branches and ATMs are linked to lower infant mortality and higher composite well‐being. Bank branches are also linked to higher life expectancy, whereas the ATM–life expectancy relationship and both indicators' relationships with undernourishment are statistically insignificant. Digital financial inclusion shows heterogeneous relationships. Debit cards are linked to lower infant mortality, higher life expectancy and a weakly significant increase in composite well‐being. Credit cards are linked to lower infant mortality but lower life expectancy and composite well‐being, and higher undernourishment. E‐banking is linked to lower infant mortality and weakly higher life expectancy, but higher undernourishment and lower composite well‐being. Green credit is linked to lower infant mortality and undernourishment and higher life expectancy and composite well‐being. The reported mediation estimates suggest favourable indirect channels via green credit for traditional banking infrastructure and debit cards, but adverse indirect channels for credit cards and e‐banking. The findings show the significance of differentiating financial instruments and the environmental orientation of debt allocation. They represent country‐level relationships rather than definitive causal effects.

title: Digital Technologies to Address Transparency and Traceability for Sustainable Supply Chain Management: A Stakeholder Perspective
abstract: ABSTRACT The concept of supply chain transparency and traceability as a crucial aspect of sustainability is gaining traction among academics, practitioners, and policymakers. In this perspective, digital technologies are recognized as essential enablers to address transparency and traceability for sustainable supply chain management in organizations. Despite the increasing global shift in digitalization in various industries, the adoption of digital technologies in the agricultural sector in developing economies remains limited. Hence, this exploratory study aims to investigate the use of digital tools enabling stakeholders to address transparency and traceability for sustainable supply chain management in the Sri Lankan tea sector. A qualitative research methodology was used and 24 semistructured interviews were conducted with 13 participants holding different positions in the Sri Lankan tea supply chain. Drawing on the resource‐based view and stakeholder theory, the study findings highlighted various digital tools as valuable resources facilitating upstream, midstream, and downstream stakeholders to address transparency and traceability for achieving economic, environmental, and social sustainability in tea supply chain operations. The study contributes to the existing literature through detailed investigation and empirical mapping of digital technologies used by supply chain actors across upstream, midstream, and downstream activities in the Sri Lankan tea supply chain. Using the perspectives and in‐depth insights of 13 stakeholders across the Sri Lankan tea supply chain, the findings present a grounded picture of how digital technologies are operationalized in a specific agricultural supply chain in a developing economy context.

title: From Green Innovation to Legitimacy: The Roles of ESG Engagement and Institutional Context in China
abstract: ABSTRACT Environmental innovation does not automatically confer legitimacy: firms must also persuade institutional audiences that their actions merit recognition. This distinction matters in state‐capitalist economies, where the state evaluates firms alongside investors and communities. Using panel data on Chinese A‐share listed firms from 2010 to 2023, we examine the association between green innovation and state‐oriented legitimacy (SOL), the mediating role of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) engagement, and the moderating role of regional institutional quality. We distinguish green innovation as a substantive activity, ESG engagement as a potential signal, and SOL as a state‐oriented legitimacy measure. Green innovation is positively associated with SOL, partly through ESG engagement. Institutional quality appears to strengthen this indirect relationship mainly through the link between innovation and ESG engagement. The findings extend research on how institutional context shapes the relationship between environmental activity, corporate signalling, and legitimacy.

title: Climate Change and Energy System Dynamics in Sub‐Saharan Africa: New Evidence From the Role of Institutional Quality
abstract: ABSTRACT Climate pressures have become an increasingly decisive force shaping the evolution of energy systems across sub‐Saharan Africa (SSA). This study examines how climate change and shocks affect energy intensity, renewable electricity output, and electricity access across 19 SSA countries from 1995 to 2023 using a high‐dimensional fixed effects estimator. The analysis introduces the Notre Dame Climate Vulnerability Index (ND‐CVI) into energy transition analysis and formalizes an institutional resilience mechanism that specifies how government effectiveness and regulatory quality moderate the climate–energy relationship through distinct governance channels. The results show that climate vulnerability persistently constrains renewable electricity generation but has weaker effects on energy intensity and electricity access in the baseline specifications. Institutional moderation is heterogeneous across energy outcomes. Government effectiveness weakens the vulnerability–renewable relationship, while regulatory quality shapes the vulnerability–access relationship. Heterogeneity analysis identifies hydro‐dependence as the key transmission channel, with the adverse renewable effect concentrated among the most hydropower‐reliant economies. Temporal comparisons reveal that climate vulnerability effects on renewable output emerged more clearly in the post‐2010 transition era, as regional renewable capacity expanded but remained climate‐sensitive. Findings are robust to alternative shock specifications, outlier adjustment, panel‐corrected standard errors, and instrumental variables estimation using lagged climate vulnerability. The results highlight the importance of renewable diversification, sequenced governance reforms, and integrating adaptation finance into long‐term energy transition strategies in SSA. Trial Registration: Not applicable

title: Unraveling the Factors of Sustainable Market Competitiveness: Strategies of Digitalization, Circular Economy, Green Finance, and Gender Equality
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite the central role of digitalization, circular economy, green finance, and gender equality in the European Union (EU) sustainability and competitiveness agendas, the mechanisms through which these factors jointly shape sustainable market competitiveness remain insufficiently understood. Existing research has widely examined these factors in isolation, whereas rare attention has been given to their combined direct, mediating, and moderating relationships grounded in the dynamic capabilities view, ecological modernization, and feminist institutionalism theories across the EU member states. Hence, this study primarily aims to examine the direct association among the outlined factors. Secondly, it examines the mediating role of circular economy between digitalization and sustainable market competitiveness, the mediating role of circular economy between green finance and sustainable market competitiveness, and the mediating role of green finance between digitalization and circular economy. Third, it seeks the moderating role of gender equality between digitalization and circular economy, the moderating role of gender equality between digitalization and green finance, and the moderating role of gender equality between green finance and circular economy across the EU nations. To this end, the study extracted country‐year level data from Eurostat and the OECD for 2014–2023, with a sample size of 270, and analyzed the data using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS‐SEM) to clarify hypothesized associations among constructs. The outcomes indicate that all the direct and mediating paths are positive and statistically significant in the defined settings. In addition, gender equality significantly moderates the relationship between digitalization and circular economy but does not significantly moderate the relationships between digitalization and green finance or between green finance and circular economy. These outcomes extend the existing literature by directing EU policymakers on how to leverage these factors in digital‐to‐green transition, clarify the conditional mechanism of gender equality, and offer evidence‐based guidance to achieve sustainable market competitiveness. The study also contributes by integrating the dynamic capabilities, ecological modernization, and feminist institutionalism theories to draw comprehensive theoretical map for the sustainable market competitiveness. Hence, this study is unique in aligning the outlined factors in a multitheoretical framework for digital‐to‐green transition to achieve sustainable market competitiveness across the EU nations.

title: How firms and NGOs align resources and knowledge to address biodiversity loss: a network perspective
When the Ground Shifts: Why Artificial Intelligence Requires Both Policy and Debate
abstract: Overview This editorial introduces the new Business & Society artificial intelligence (AI) policy developed through an 8-month collaborative process. The policy builds on a central premise: humans remain in the driver’s seat while AI serves as an assistant, and is guided by four core principles: Accountability , Integrity , Responsibility , and Transparency (AIRT). Accordingly, we establish boundaries between acceptable and prohibited practices of authors, reviewers, and editors, and call for disclosure of all AI use by authors. Beyond presenting the policy, we reflect on difficult questions that emerged during its development, particularly regarding transparency, disclosure, and the process of policymaking itself. Rather than claiming to resolve these issues, we explain the reasoning behind the choices made. We also acknowledge unresolved challenges related to governance and the rapid evolution of AI technologies, and invite ongoing dialog on the environmental, social, and institutional implications of AI for scholarship.

title: Deriving value from mobile shopping apps: mediating and moderating mechanisms across countries
abstract: Purpose This study focuses on how consumers derive value from mobile shopping apps, investigating how service quality dimensions are associated with utilitarian, hedonic and social value perceptions and how these value perceptions, in turn, relate to app loyalty. Grounded in Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-O-R) theory, it empirically tests a model of direct, mediating and moderating effects across consumers in the USA, UK and UAE. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 543 shopping app users in the USA, UK and UAE. The proposed model was tested using structural equation modelling, with separate structural models estimated for each country to allow detailed within-country examination and cross-national comparison. Mediation and moderation analyses were also conducted. Findings The results provide empirical evidence of associations that are consistent with the notion that service quality dimensions shape value perceptions, with significant variations across countries. Efficiency and contact are consistently associated with multiple value facets across all three countries, while fulfilment and responsiveness are context-specific, primarily in the UAE. All value dimensions are positively associated with app loyalty and mediate the association between service quality and app loyalty. The positive association between hedonic value and app loyalty is consistently stronger at higher levels of intrinsic enjoyment. The pattern of significant pathways differs across the three national contexts. Originality/value This study provides a cross-national investigation of how established quality–value–loyalty pathways operate across three culturally distinct markets: the USA, UK and UAE. By comparing these regions, it reveals where the associations between service quality and value remain consistent and how the associations between utilitarian, hedonic and social value and app loyalty differ.

title: ‘Flying under the radar’: job crafting when menopause disrupts neurodivergent coping
abstract: Human Resource Management increasingly recognises the importance of job crafting, which relies on personal structures of coping. This study foregrounds workplace job crafting using a critical case approach, focusing on neurodivergent individuals whose coping mechanisms may be destabilised during menopause. Qualitative data from semi-structured interviews with 45 neurodivergent women experiencing menopause symptoms (UK and US) were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Findings provide insight into how intersecting vulnerabilities shape person-led workplace adaptation. Specifically, neurodivergent women experiencing menopause symptoms were found to engage in different forms of avoidance job crafting (behavioural avoidance demand crafting, behavioural avoidance resource crafting, cognitive avoidance demand crafting). Moreover, a newly identified preservation orientation drives a combination of avoidance and approach job crafting, evidenced by crafting strategies that primarily focus preservation, or maintaining the status quo, to align personal resources within maintaining job performance. This article contributes to the job crafting literature by demonstrating distinctive job crafting practices of individuals whose life-long coping strategies (of neurodivergence) are temporarily and transitionally destabilised (by menopause symptoms). Organisations have a critical role to support potentially stigmatised employees, thereby nurturing inclusive human resources support policies that provide support to individuals experiencing multiple stigmas.
